summary: Describes methods for extending the useful life of symmetric keys, since only a limited amount of data can be safely encrypted under one key. It offers two kinds of re-keying based on hash functions and on block ciphers, usable with modes such as CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB, and OMAC. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8645 is a catalogue of ways to stretch the life of a symmetric encryption key. Instead of throwing the key away and negotiating a new one, the key is transformed into a series of shorter-lived keys that each protect a slice of the data. The RFC gives the exact formulas for each construction and says when to use each one.

questions: how to rekey with block ciphers
when should you use external vs internal re-keying
subtitle: Ways to let one symmetric key protect much more data than it safely could on its own.

tldr.problem: Only a limited amount of data can safely be encrypted under a single symmetric key, and renegotiating a fresh key often costs a round trip and public-key work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two families of re-keying. External re-keying derives a series of frame keys from the initial key at the protocol level, and internal re-keying transforms a section key every N bits inside the encryption mode itself.
tldr.outcome: Both families remove the side-channel limit that normally binds a key, leaving only the combinatorial limit of the mode, and the RFC lists named constructions for each so that a protocol can pick one.

today: RFC 8645 is an Informational document from August 2019 that represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group. No RFC obsoletes or updates it, so the constructions it names remain the reference list for extending the life of symmetric keys.

sections.title: Why a Key Cannot Be Used Forever
sections.content:
A certain maximum amount of data can be safely encrypted under a single key, an amount the document calls the key lifetime. The need for such a limitation is dictated by three families of cryptanalysis. The first are methods based on the combinatorial properties of the block cipher mode of operation; they do not depend on the underlying block cipher, and common mode restrictions derived from them are of order 2^(n/2), where n is the block size. The second are methods based on side-channel analysis; in most cases they do not depend on the mode used and only weakly depend on the cipher features, and the limitations they impose are usually the most restrictive. The third are methods based on the properties of the block cipher, such as linear and differential cryptanalysis, but for secure block ciphers those bounds are roughly the natural bounds of 2^n and are dominated by the other two, so they are excluded from consideration.

It is therefore important to replace a key when the total size of the processed plaintext under it approaches the limit, with a specific value chosen to leave a safety margin for protocol security. If L is the key lifetime limitation in a protocol and all messages have length m, the number of messages q that can be processed with a single key K must satisfy m * q <= L.

The simplest solution is a regular renegotiation of the initial key after this threshold amount of data. That reduces total performance, because it usually entails termination of application data transmission, additional service messages, the use of a random number generator and many other calculations, including resource-intensive public key cryptography. For protocols based on block ciphers or stream ciphers, a more efficient way to increase the key lifetime is to use re-keying mechanisms. This document considers block ciphers only; the mechanisms typical for stream ciphers are beyond its scope.

Re-keying can be applied at several levels. At the block cipher level it is known as fresh re-keying, but it is highly inefficient because the key changes after each message block, and it can change the block cipher's internal structure and so require an additional security analysis for each particular block cipher. At the block cipher mode of operation level it is internal re-keying. At the protocol level above the mode of operation it is external re-keying.

The RFC presents both of the latter. External re-keying is performed by the protocol and is independent of the underlying block cipher and the mode of operation; in the parallel case the data processing keys K^1, K^2 and so on are generated directly from the initial key K independently of each other, and in the serial case every data processing key depends on a secret state that is updated after each new key is generated. Internal re-keying is built into the mode and depends heavily on the properties of the mode and the block size.
sections.plainLanguage: There is always a point where one key has protected so much data that using it is no longer safe. The usual response is to negotiate a brand-new key, which costs a round trip and heavy public-key work. This RFC describes the alternative: derive a series of keys from the original one, each used for a limited stretch of data, so no renegotiation is needed.

sections.title: Choosing Between the Two Kinds
sections.content:
External re-keying assumes that a key is transformed after encrypting a limited number of entire messages. It is chosen at the protocol level, regardless of the underlying block cipher or encryption mode, and is recommended for protocols that process relatively short messages or that have a way to divide a long message into manageable pieces. Through external re-keying the number of messages that can be securely processed with a single initial key is substantially increased without a loss of message length.

Its advantages are that it increases the lifetime of an initial key by increasing the number of messages processed with it, that it has minimal impact on performance when the number of messages processed under one initial key is sufficiently large, and that it provides forward and backward security of the data processing keys. Its disadvantage is that with restrictive key lifetime limitations the message sizes can become obstructive, because it may be impossible to process sufficiently large messages, so additional fragmentation may be needed at the protocol level. For example, if the key lifetime L is 1 GB and the message length m is 3 GB, that message cannot be processed as a whole and should be divided into three fragments processed separately.

Internal re-keying assumes that a key is transformed during each separate message processing. Such procedures are integrated into the base modes of operation, so every internal re-keying mechanism is defined for the particular operation mode and block size. It is recommended for protocols that process long messages: the size of each single message can be substantially increased without loss in the number of messages that can be securely processed with a single initial key. Its advantages are that it increases the lifetime of an initial key by increasing the size of the messages processed with it, that it has minimal impact on performance, that internal re-keying mechanisms without a master key do not affect short-message transformation at all, and that it is transparent, working like any mode of operation without requiring changes to initialization vectors or a restart of MACing. Its disadvantages are that a specific method cannot be chosen independently of a mode of operation, and that internal re-keying mechanisms without a master key do not provide backward security of the data processing keys.

Any block cipher mode with internal re-keying can be used with any external re-keying mechanism, and such joint usage increases both the number of messages processed with one initial key and their maximum possible size. If an adversary has access to the data processing interface, using the same cryptographic primitives for data processing and for the re-keying transformation decreases code size but can lead to vulnerabilities, because a chosen-plaintext attack may lead to the compromise of the following keys. Using different primitives, for example a block cipher for data processing and a hash for re-keying, removes that risk, but then the security of the whole scheme cannot be reduced to standard notions such as a pseudorandom function or permutation, so security estimations become more difficult.

The RFC sums up the guidance. If a protocol assumes processing of long records, internal re-keying should be used; a protocol that processes a significant number of ordered records that can be considered a single data stream may also use it. For protocols that allow out-of-order delivery and lost records, external re-keying should be used, because such records cannot be considered a single data stream, and if the records are also long enough, internal re-keying should be used during each separate message processing. For external re-keying, hash function-based re-keying should be used when it is desirable to separate the transformations used for data processing and key updates, parallel external re-keying when parallel data processing is required, and external tree-based re-keying when restrictive key lifetime limitations are present. For internal re-keying, internal re-keying with a master key should be used when forward and backward security of the data processing keys is desirable and additional key material can be easily obtained for the data-processing stage.
sections.plainLanguage: External re-keying suits protocols that send many small records, because it multiplies the number of records a key can cover. Internal re-keying suits protocols that send one large record, because it splits the record up and changes key as it goes. A protocol with both kinds of traffic can use both at once.

sections.title: External Re-keying and Its Named Constructions
sections.content:
External re-keying increases the initial key lifetime by transforming a data processing key, the frame key, after processing a limited number of entire messages. These mechanisms use the initial key K only for frame key generation and never use it directly for data processing, and they operate outside the base modes of operation without changing them at all.

The principle is that the key lifetime limitation induced by side-channel analysis, L1, and the limitation induced by the combinatorial properties of the mode, L2, are separate. As L1 is usually much stronger than L2, without re-keying only q1 messages of length m can be processed, where q1 * m <= L1. If the frame keys are generated so that the leakage of a previous frame key has no impact on the following one, the side-channel limitation is switched off, and the resulting limitation of the initial key can be calculated on the basis of a new combinatorial limitation L2', which is larger than L2.

To illustrate, take a protocol whose message size is 1 KB, with L1 = 128 MB and L2 = 1 TB. Without external re-keying the initial key must be renegotiated after 128 MB / 1 KB = 131072 messages. With external re-keying the L1 limitation goes off, so the resulting limitation L2' can be set to more than 1 TB, and more than 1 TB / 1 KB = 2^30 messages can be processed before renegotiation. That is 8192 times greater than the number possible without re-keying.

How many messages a frame key covers can be decided in three ways. The explicit approach picks q_i so that the total size of the messages processed is at most L but adding the next one would exceed it; this uses the frame key almost optimally but can only be applied when messages cannot be lost or reordered, as with TLS records. The implicit approach sets q_i = L / m_max, assuming every message has the maximum length, which can make the amount of data processed considerably less than the limit but works when messages may be lost or reordered, as with DTLS records. A third option organizes the key change using the Protected Point to Point solution, building a protected tunnel between the endpoints so that the key update can be passed across safely, which can be useful when the adversary should not detect the key change during protocol evaluation.

Five named constructions are given. ExtParallelC is a parallel construction based on a key derivation function on a block cipher, generating t frame keys as the concatenation of the encryptions of the counters 0, 1 and so on under the initial key. ExtParallelH is the parallel construction based on a hash function, using HKDF-Expand with a protocol-defined label. ExtKeyTree is the tree-based construction, a generalization of parallel re-keying in which the initial key is the root of a tree of derived keys whose leaves are the frame keys; it can be viewed as the tree generalization of the GGM construction, and similar structures are used in the one-way tree mechanism and in the AES Derived Unique Key Per Transaction standard. ExtSerialC is the serial construction based on a block cipher, where each frame key is computed from a secret state that is itself derived from the previous state, so the keys form a chain. ExtSerialH is the serial construction based on a hash function, using HKDF-Expand with two different protocol-defined labels. Serial constructions cannot be computed in parallel, but they may be preferred if additional forward secrecy is desirable: if all keys are securely deleted after use, the compromise of a current secret state does not compromise the earlier ones.

On additional entropy, the RFC notes that in many cases mixing extra entropy into re-keying will not increase security and may give a false sense of it, since good key derivation functions do not require additional entropy for the quality of the keys. It can still help in the specific case of a time-limited but complete breach where an adversary can reach the frame key generation interface but cannot reveal the master keys, for example when the master keys are held in a hardware security module.
sections.plainLanguage: External re-keying works by deriving a sequence of frame keys from the initial key, and using each frame key for a bounded stretch of messages. Two shapes are described: parallel, where every frame key is derived straight from the initial key and can be computed independently, and serial, where each key depends on the previous one, which costs serial computation but limits the damage from a later compromise. There is also a tree-shaped variant for very tight limits.

sections.title: Internal Re-keying and Section Keys
sections.content:
Internal re-keying increases the key lifetime by transforming a data processing key, the section key, during each separate message processing. Each message is processed starting with the same key, the first section key, and each section key is updated after processing N bits of the message. The RFC provides two mechanisms, ACPKM (Advanced Cryptographic Prolongation of Key Material) and ACPKM-Master, which do not use and do use a master key respectively. They are integrated into the base modes of operation and form new modes of operation, which is why they are called internal.

The additional parameter is the section size N, measured in bits and fixed within a specific protocol based on the requirements of system capacity and key lifetime. N MUST be divisible by the block size n. The mechanism works as follows. The input message M of length m is divided into l = ceil(m / N) sections. The first section of each message is processed with the section key K^1 = K. To process the (i+1)-th section, the next section key is calculated as K^{i+1} = ACPKM(K^i) = MSB_k(E_{K^i}(D_1) | ... | E_{K^i}(D_J)), where J = ceil(k/n) and the D_j are taken from a fixed 1024-bit constant D whose octets run from 80 to ff, so that D_1 through D_J are pairwise different for any allowed n and k values. The highest bit of each octet of that constant is 1, which matters because, together with a message length limitation, it prevents collisions of block cipher permutation inputs in cases where key transformation and message processing meet.

Because only one section of each message is processed with a given section key, the side-channel limitation L1 goes off, leaving the new combinatorial limitation L2'. The RFC illustrates this with L1 = 128 MB, L2 = 10 TB and a maximum message size of 32 MB: without internal re-keying the initial key would have to be renegotiated after only four messages, whereas with a section size N = 1 MB more than 128 MB / 1 MB = 128 messages can be processed before renegotiation.

Several concrete modes are then defined by applying the mechanism to a base mode. CTR-ACPKM extends CTR and is usable with 64 <= n <= 512, 128 <= k <= 512, a counter part of c bits where 32 <= c <= 3/4 n and c is a multiple of 8, and a maximum message size of n * 2^(c-1); the initial counter nonce for each message encrypted under a given initial key must be chosen uniquely. GCM-ACPKM extends GCM and requires n in {128, 256}, 128 <= k <= 512, a counter part of c bits where 1/4 n <= c <= 1/2 n and c is a multiple of 8, and a maximum message size of min{n * (2^(c-1) - 2), 2^(n/2) - 1}. Further modes cover CTR, GCM, CBC and CFB encryption and OMAC authentication in their ACPKM-Master versions, which add a master key from which the initial key is derived.
sections.plainLanguage: Internal re-keying sits inside the encryption mode. The message is cut into sections of a fixed size, and the key is transformed between sections, so no single key ever covers more than one section's worth of data. The RFC gives the exact transformation, the required section size, and the concrete modes that result from applying it to CTR, GCM, CBC, CFB and OMAC.

sections.title: Using Both Together
sections.content:
External re-keying and internal re-keying each have advantages and disadvantages. External re-keying essentially limits the message length, while with internal re-keying the section size, which can be chosen as large as operational properties allow, limits the number of separate messages. The choice therefore depends on the features of the protocol. Some protocols need the advantages of both: for example a protocol that mainly transmits short messages but must also support very long messages. In such situations it is necessary to use external and internal re-keying jointly, since the two techniques negate each other's disadvantages. Any mechanism from the external section can be used with any mechanism from the internal section.

The RFC works an example through with the GCM-ACPKM mode and external serial re-keying based on a key derivation function on a hash function. The number of messages in each frame, the frame size in the implicit approach to key lifetime control, is called q. The section size N for internal re-keying and the frame size q for external re-keying must be chosen so that q * N does not exceed the key lifetime limitation L.

Suppose that t messages, each with its initial counter nonce, plaintext and additional authenticated data, will be processed before renegotiation. For each message the algorithm is: set j = ceil(i / q); compute the frame key K^j = ExtSerialH(K, j); then encrypt with C_i | T_i = GCM-ACPKM-Encrypt(N, K^j, ICN_i, P_i, A_i). Nonces used under the same frame key must be unique for each message.
sections.plainLanguage: Neither mechanism alone suits every protocol, so the RFC allows them to be stacked: the outer layer decides which key handles a run of messages, and the inner layer rotates the key inside each message. The two sizes must be chosen so that their product stays under the key's limit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Re-keying should be used to increase the a priori security properties of ciphers in hostile environments, for example with side-channel adversaries. If efficient attacks on a cipher are known, the cipher must not be used, so re-keying cannot be used as a patch for vulnerable ciphers. The base cipher properties must be well analyzed, because the security of the re-keying mechanisms is based on the security of a block cipher as a pseudorandom function.

Re-keying is not intended to solve any post-quantum security issues for symmetric cryptography. The reduction of security caused by Grover's algorithm is not connected with the size of the plaintext transformed by a cipher, since only a negligible amount of material is needed, and the aim of re-keying is to limit the size of the plaintext transformed under one initial key.

Re-keying can provide backward security only if the previous key material is securely deleted after use by all parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Re-keying is not a way to make a weak cipher usable, and it does not help against a quantum computer. The one thing it needs from the parties is that they actually erase the old key material once they have moved on to the next key, otherwise an old key recovered later still exposes the data it covered.

items.title: ExtParallelC
items.text: Parallel, based on a key derivation function on a block cipher. Frame keys come straight from the initial key and can be computed independently.

items.title: ExtParallelH
items.text: Parallel, based on HKDF-Expand with a protocol-defined label. Frame keys come straight from the initial key.

items.title: ExtKeyTree
items.text: Tree-based. The initial key is the root of a tree of derived keys and the frame keys are its leaves.

items.title: ExtSerialC
items.text: Serial, based on a block cipher. Each frame key comes from a secret state derived from the previous one.

items.title: ExtSerialH
items.text: Serial, based on HKDF-Expand with two different protocol-defined labels.
